ai-clothing-try-on-guide.body_html:
AI clothing try-on uses your own photo to generate an image of you wearing a different outfit, so you can judge the overall look before you put anything on or spend money. It is a style preview, not a fitting room. It can help with color, silhouette and mood, but it cannot tell you how a garment will actually fit your body. This guide explains how to get a useful preview, how to judge it honestly, and how to turn it into real outfit decisions.

What AI clothing try-on is (and what it isn't)

How an AI preview of you in an outfit works, in plain terms

In general terms, you give a tool a photo of yourself and an idea of the outfit. The AI then generates a new image that shows a version of you in that look. Different tools approach this differently, so results vary in quality and realism. What they share is that the output is a generated image, an educated visual guess, rather than a measurement of your body or a simulation of a real garment.

A style preview vs. a fitting-room test

A fitting room tells you whether a specific garment works on your body. An AI preview tells you whether an idea is worth pursuing. Think of it as a mood board that happens to include your face and general frame.

What an AI image can't tell you: exact fit, sizing and fabric drape

An AI preview can help withAn AI preview can't tell you
Overall vibe of a look (polished, relaxed, edgy)Exact garment fit or sizing
How a color palette feels with your hair and complexionHow a fabric stretches, wrinkles or breathes
The general silhouette: oversized, tailored, croppedHow a specific brand's cut sits on your shoulders, hips or length
Whether a style direction appeals to youHow clothes move when you walk, sit or reach

Why preview an outfit with AI before you commit

Testing a new style or aesthetic without buying anything

If you are curious about Old Money, Streetwear, Y2K or Minimalist, a preview lets you see whether the direction feels like you before you build a wardrobe around it. For example, a quiet-luxury look might be a camel coat, cream knit and dark trousers, while a streetwear look might be a boxy tee, relaxed cargos and chunky sneakers. Seeing each on yourself is often more telling than scrolling through someone else's photos.

Narrowing down options when you're torn between looks

When you have three outfits in mind and can't pick, previews turn a vague feeling into a side-by-side comparison. You may notice quickly that one option looks heavy, one looks washed out, and one simply feels right.

Planning an outfit for an event ahead of time

For a wedding, interview or date night, previewing a few directions days in advance gives you time to adjust shoes, layers or colors rather than scrambling an hour before you leave.

Set up a photo that gives a realistic preview

The quality of your starting photo shapes everything that follows. A few habits make previews easier to judge:

Use a clear, well-lit, head-to-toe photo that includes your shoes

Full length matters because proportion, the relationship between top, bottom and shoes, is a big part of whether an outfit works. Soft daylight from a window or open shade is usually more flattering and consistent than a harsh overhead bulb.

Stand straight on, with a plain background and no heavy filters

Face the camera with your arms relaxed at your sides, and have someone take the photo at about chest height, or prop the phone up. Skip beauty filters, since they can change how your features and skin color look, which makes it harder to judge color later.

Why a fitted, simple base outfit can help

Baggy layers or a heavy coat hide your outline, which makes it harder for anyone, you included, to judge proportion from the photo. As general advice, wearing something simple and reasonably fitted, such as a plain tee and straight jeans, gives a clearer base to compare against.

How to try outfits on yourself with AI, step by step

These steps are general and apply to most AI preview tools. For what FitCheck AI offers specifically, see the app section further down.

Step 1: Pick the occasion and the feeling you want

Decide where you are going and how you want to come across: sharp for work, relaxed for a casual weekend, a bit dressier for date night. This keeps you from generating random looks that don't serve a purpose.

Step 2: Choose two or three outfit directions to compare

Make the options meaningfully different. For a work day, try a tonal navy suit set, a light-gray blazer with white tee and dark jeans, and a knit polo with tailored chinos. Three nearly identical options teach you very little.

Step 3: Generate your previews and keep the best ones

Results vary from image to image, so look at more than one. Keep the ones that look most natural and set aside those with obvious glitches.

Step 4: Compare them side by side instead of judging one in isolation

One image on its own is easy to like. Lined up next to the others, weak points show: a color that dulls your face, a hem that cuts you at an awkward spot, a look that feels like a costume.

How to judge an AI try-on image honestly

Color: does the palette suit your skin tone, hair and eye color?

Look at the color closest to your face first. If a shade makes you look tired or washed out, try a different one near the neckline. Warm-leaning complexions often look good in olive, camel, rust and cream, while cool-leaning ones often favor navy, charcoal, burgundy and icy tones, though these are tendencies, not rules. If you are unsure of your own coloring, our guide on how to find your skin depth and undertone is a good starting point.

Proportion: where do the top, bottom and shoes break up your frame?

Notice where the outfit divides your body. A common styling approach is a roughly one-third to two-thirds split, such as a cropped jacket with high-waisted trousers, or a tucked top with a longer bottom. If everything ends at the widest point of your hips, or the look feels boxy all over, try balancing a loose piece with a fitted one.

Occasion and dress code: does it fit where you're going?

An outfit can look great and still be wrong for the setting. Ask whether the formality, coverage and shoes suit the event and the weather.

Realism check: spot over-smoothed fabric, impossible drape or an unrealistically perfect fit

Be skeptical when fabric looks too smooth, seams vanish, patterns warp, hands or accessories look distorted, or the garment fits with zero wrinkles. These are signs the image may be flattering you in a way a real garment might not. Treat the preview as an idea, not a promise.

Remember it's one AI opinion, not an objective verdict

An AI image or score is a second opinion, not a professional stylist's judgment and not an objective truth. Your comfort, taste and the context matter as much as anything the screen shows.

From preview to real life

Match the preview to clothes you already own before buying anything new

Take a preview you like and try recreating it from your closet. A rust-colored top you liked in a preview might be approximated by a terracotta tee you already have. If you can build most of a look from what you own, you will know exactly what, if anything, is worth adding. A tidy wardrobe makes this much easier, and our 6-step closet organization method can help.

Do a mirror test and a photo test in the real outfit

Put the real outfit on, check yourself in a full-length mirror, and take a photo. Cameras and mirrors reveal different things. For a deeper checklist, see how to tell if your outfit looks good.

Check actual size, stretch and comfort in person

Sit down, raise your arms, and walk around. Check the shoulders, the rise, the sleeve and hem length, and whether you can wear it all day. No preview can answer these questions.

Common reasons a preview looks different in person

Lighting and photo angle

Warm indoor light, a low camera angle or a wide-angle lens can change how colors and proportions read. Compare previews and real photos taken in similar light.

Fabric weight, texture and how it moves

A stiff cotton, a clingy knit and a flowy viscose can look similar in a generated image yet behave very differently on the body.

Sizing and cut differences between brands

A medium from one label can fit like a small or large from another. A preview doesn't know the cut, so always check a brand's own size information and return policy when you buy clothes elsewhere.

Styling details the image can't show

Tailoring, cuffs, a French tuck, a belt, a watch or layered jewelry can make the same pieces look sharper or sloppier. Treat these as the finishing step after you pick a direction.

How FitCheck AI can help you try clothing virtually

From your own photo, it generates AI images of you in different outfits, along with AI-generated fashion images and styling previews. You can also explore aesthetics like Old Money, Y2K, Streetwear, Vintage, Minimalist and Quiet Luxury. These images are AI-generated style previews and do not show exact garment fit or sizing. The app is for style previews and outfit feedback, not for buying clothes.

Once you have a real outfit on, you can take or upload a full-body photo for an AI outfit score and a style breakdown covering color match, proportion and balance, with easy ways to improve. Live FitCheck lets you check an outfit live with the camera, and you can save your top-scoring looks to a digital closet and plan outfits ahead for work, events or date nights. The scores are an AI second opinion, not a professional verdict. For details on how photos are handled, see the app's privacy policy.

Here is one way you could combine these features. Start with a full-body photo of yourself, then look at AI-generated images of yourself in a few different outfits or aesthetics. Pick the direction you like best and put together a version from your own clothes. Then take a full-body photo of the real outfit for an outfit score and style breakdown, and save it to your digital closet if it scores well. Treat each step as a starting point, not a final verdict.

A simple way to put it all together

Preview two or three directions, shortlist the one that feels right in color and proportion, rebuild it from clothes you own, then confirm it in a mirror. That sequence keeps AI where it is most useful, generating ideas, and leaves fit and comfort to the real world.

color-matching-clothes-for-women.body_html:
The easiest way to match colors in a women's outfit is to build on one or two neutrals, add a single supporting color, and keep any bright shade to a small accent. Colors don't have to be identical to go together. They just need to feel related through hue, depth or intensity. This guide covers the rules, example combinations, and fixes for when an outfit looks off.

Color matching basics: what "goes together" means

Matching vs. coordinating

Exact matching, like a navy top with navy pants in the same dye, is rare and often looks flat. Coordinating is more flexible: the colors share something, so they look chosen. A cream blouse with camel trousers and a brown belt is coordinated, not matched.

Three things that make a combination work

  • Hue: the color family itself (blue, green, red, and so on).
  • Depth: how light or dark a color is. Light blue and navy are the same hue at different depths.
  • Intensity: how bright or muted it is. Hot pink is intense. Dusty rose is muted.

When two colors clash, one of these is usually off. Two intense colors compete, and two colors of the same depth blur together. Changing just one of the three often fixes it.

Start with neutrals: the easiest base

Your building blocks

Black, white, gray, navy, beige, camel, brown and olive all work as bases. Most wardrobes are built on three or four of them.

Neutrals that combine well

  • Navy with camel or cream
  • Black with gray or white
  • Cream with chocolate brown
  • Olive with beige or tan
  • Gray with navy or soft pink

Why layering several neutrals works

An outfit of beige, cream and tan in different textures looks richer than one flat shade. The variation in depth adds interest without adding "color," so it reads as intentional.

Color wheel basics for outfits, without the jargon

Monochrome

Wear different shades of one color: a pale blue shirt, mid-blue jeans and a navy blazer. Vary the depth so the pieces don't blend into a single block.

Analogous

Neighboring colors on the wheel create a soft, harmonious look. Examples are olive with mustard, teal with navy, or blush with coral. These pairings usually feel easy because the colors are related.

Complementary

Opposites, like blue and orange, purple and yellow, or red and green, create strong contrast. To tone them down, make one muted (rust with denim blue) or use one as a small accent. Burgundy and forest green work well because both are deep.

Neutral plus one accent

This is the simplest way to wear a bold color. A cobalt top with cream trousers and tan sandals, or a camel coat over a red scarf and black jeans, lets one color do the talking.

A simple formula for how many colors to wear

Dominant, supporting, accent

A loose 60-30-10 guide works well: about 60% one dominant color, 30% a supporting color, and 10% a small accent in a bag, scarf, shoes or jewelry. That makes about three colors, and neutrals often don't count as a full color. Treat it as a loose guide, not a strict rule.

When to stop at two

If you're wearing a strong print or a bright color, keep everything else to one or two neutrals. Two colors plus neutral accessories is usually a safe choice.

Example outfits

  • Work: navy trousers (60), white shirt (30), a camel bag and belt (10).
  • Casual: light-wash jeans (60), an olive tee (30), white sneakers and a tan crossbody bag (10).
  • Evening: a black dress (60), a burgundy clutch (10) and gold jewelry, with a gray wrap (30) if you need a layer.

Easy color combinations for women to try

Start withPairs well withWhy it works
NavyWhite, camel, blush, light grayDark base with light or warm contrast
BeigeOlive, brown, soft blue, whiteSoft base that suits earthy and cool colors
OliveCream, rust, mustard, denimMuted green with warm or neutral partners
BurgundyNavy, gray, blush, forest greenDeep shade that pairs with other deep or soft tones
BlackAlmost anything, including red, cream and grayStrong depth that makes other colors stand out

Softer and bolder pairings

Pastels and muted tones, such as lavender with sage or powder blue with cream, look calm together because their intensity is similar. For bolder looks, keep depth or intensity balanced. Cobalt with emerald can work if both are equally saturated, and hot pink with red works best when one is a small accent.

Tricky pairings and how to adjust

If two colors fight, add a neutral buffer between them. Red and pink, or orange and purple, are easier with a white, denim or black piece separating them. You can also shift one color to a deeper or paler shade.

Mixing prints and patterns by color

Pull one color from the print

Choose a shade that appears in the print and repeat it in a solid. A floral skirt with pink and green can pair with a plain green top and pink earrings.

Pair a print with solids

Let the print be the star and keep the rest simple. A striped navy-and-white top works with camel trousers or white jeans.

Mix two prints

Use a shared color but different scales. For example, a small polka dot blouse in navy and white pairs better with wide navy stripes than with another small pattern.

Shoes, bags, belts and jewelry: match or contrast?

Echo a color rather than match it exactly

Shoes and bag don't have to match. It looks more natural if they are in the same family, like tan shoes with a caramel bag, or if one echoes a color elsewhere in the outfit. Slightly different shades can look better than near-misses.

Neutral accessories are a reliable default

Black, tan, white or metallic accessories sit comfortably with most outfits. If your clothes are bold, keep accessories quiet.

Mixing metals and warm and cool tones

Mixing gold and silver is widely accepted if it looks deliberate. Wear a few pieces of each, or use a two-tone piece to link them. You can also combine warm shades like rust and mustard with cool ones like navy, as long as depth and intensity are balanced.

Choosing colors that flatter you

Loose starting points

Skin undertone, depth and natural contrast (how different your hair, skin and eyes are from each other) can guide which shades look good near your face. If you're unsure of your undertone, this skin tone guide explains how to find your depth and undertone for style purposes.

Near the face vs. the lower half

The shade near your face matters most. If a color doesn't suit you, wear it as trousers, a skirt or shoes, and put a favorite color at the neckline.

Comfort matters more than rules

Strict "season" rules are only a loose guide. If you love a color and feel good in it, it's a good choice. This is general style guidance, not professional color analysis.

Why your outfit still looks off

  • Everything is the same depth. Add a lighter or darker piece, such as a white tee under a mid-tone cardigan.
  • Two brights compete. Keep one bright, and make the other neutral or muted.
  • A color washes you out. Move it away from your face and put a more flattering shade at the neckline.
  • Lighting changes everything. Store lights, daylight and phone photos show colors differently, so check an outfit in natural light before you go.

Turn color matching into a habit

Sort your clothes by color family and you'll quickly see which neutrals you lack and which colors you overbuy. This closet organization method shows how. Note the combinations that worked so you can repeat them. Before you leave the house, take 30 seconds to check the formula: one dominant color, one supporting color, one accent. For a wider checklist, see how to tell if your outfit looks good.

How FitCheck AI can help you check your color combinations

If you'd like a second opinion, FitCheck AI is a free Android app. Take or upload a clear, well-lit, head-to-toe photo with shoes, and it gives an outfit score and a style breakdown covering color match, proportion and balance, with suggestions such as switching shoes or adjusting color contrast. Live FitCheck lets you check an outfit live with the camera, with outfit rating, color analysis, matching and styling suggestions. You can read more on the AI outfit checker page. Scores and suggestions are AI opinion and meant as a starting point, not an objective or professional verdict. Trust your own eye and comfort first. You can also save favorite looks in the digital closet and plan outfits ahead.

faqs.question: How many colors are too many in one outfit?

faqs.answer: Beige pairs well with olive, brown, soft blue and white. Olive works with cream, rust, mustard and denim. Burgundy looks good with navy, gray, blush and forest green. In each case, vary the depth so pieces don't blend together.

does-my-outfit-look-good.body_html:
Your outfit probably looks good if it fits the way the pieces were designed to, the colors and shapes work together, it suits where you're going, and you feel comfortable in it. If you're asking "does my outfit look good?", the fastest way to find out is to check those things one at a time instead of judging the whole look at once. This guide gives you a fair way to look at yourself, a 7-point checklist, and quick fixes for the most common problems.

Start with what "good" actually means

"Does it look good?" is really several questions bundled together. Separating them makes the answer much easier to find.

Three separate questions

  • Does it fit? Are the garments sitting where they should, without pulling, gaping or swamping you?
  • Does it work together? Do the colors, textures and shapes look like one outfit rather than separate pieces?
  • Does it suit the occasion? Is the formality right for the place, the people and the weather?

An outfit can pass one test and fail another. A well-fitted suit is wrong for a beach wedding, and a perfectly coordinated outfit is still a bad choice if the trousers dig in when you sit down.

Comfort and feeling like yourself count too

If you keep tugging at a hem or adjusting a neckline, it shows in how you carry yourself. An outfit that is slightly less "perfect" on paper but that you feel at ease in often looks better in real life. Treat comfort as part of the check, not an afterthought.

Set up a fair check: mirror test and photo test

A quick glance in a hallway mirror hides a lot. A slightly more careful setup gives you a much more honest read.

Full-length mirror, good light, shoes on

Put on the shoes you'll actually wear, stand a few steps back from a full-length mirror, and use daylight or bright, even light. Judging the outfit without shoes changes the proportions of trousers, skirts and dresses, so don't skip them.

Take a head-to-toe photo and look at it like it's someone else's

Photos flatten an outfit and give you distance. Look at the picture and ask what a stranger would notice first. If the answer is a wrinkle, a clashing color or a bunched waistband, that's what to fix.

Check the side and back, then sit, reach and walk

Turn sideways and look at the back. Then sit down, raise your arms and take a few steps. Check whether the shirt rides up, the waistband digs in, or the hem drags. These are the things other people see that you don't see head-on.

Photo tips (general photography advice)

These are general photography habits that tend to give a truer picture of an outfit, whatever camera or app you use:

  • Use even light and avoid strong backlighting.
  • Stand against a plain background where possible.
  • Hold the camera around waist or chest height, so legs aren't distorted.
  • Include your whole body and shoes, and skip filters.

A 7-point checklist to judge your outfit

Go through these in order. You don't need to pass every point perfectly; you're looking for the one or two things that pull the outfit down.

1. Fit

  • Shoulder seams on jackets and shirts should sit near the edge of your shoulder, unless the oversized look is deliberate.
  • Sleeves should end at the wrist on a fitted shirt, or look clearly intentional if rolled or cropped.
  • Trousers should hang cleanly. A small stack or slight break at the shoe is fine; puddling over the shoe usually looks unplanned.
  • Look for pulling across buttons, bunching at the waist, or gaping at the neckline.

2. Proportion

The easiest rule is to balance volume: pair something roomy with something more streamlined. An oversized sweater works well with slim or straight trousers. Wide-leg trousers usually look best with a fitted or tucked top. Also notice where hems and waistlines fall. A cropped jacket over a high-rise bottom looks deliberate, while a hem that stops at an awkward point on the leg can feel unplanned. If something feels off, try moving the hem or waistline slightly and compare.

3. Color

A reliable starting point is one neutral base plus two or three colors in total. Examples that rarely fail:

  • Navy trousers, white tee, tan shoes.
  • Olive pants, cream knit, brown boots.
  • Black jeans, grey sweater, one burgundy accessory.

Also check contrast. High contrast (black with white) looks sharp, while low contrast (beige with cream) looks soft. Neither is wrong, but a muddy middle, such as grey and washed-out navy, can read flat. If a color near your face looks dull on you, it can help to understand your skin tone depth and undertone, though this is a style preference, not a rule.

4. Texture, pattern and busyness

Aim for one focal point. If you have a bold print, keep everything else quiet. Mixing patterns can work when they differ in scale, such as a thin stripe with a large check, but stacking several loud things leads to the "too busy" feeling. Mixing textures, like denim with knit or leather with cotton, adds interest without adding noise.

5. Shoes and accessories

Shoes set the formality of the whole outfit. Clean white sneakers with tailored trousers read relaxed, while loafers or leather boots read polished. A belt, bag, watch or jewelry should either match the formality or add one small accent. If you're wearing three statement accessories, remove one.

6. Condition and grooming

Wrinkles, lint, scuffed shoes, loose threads and fraying hems cheapen an otherwise good outfit. Check that your hair is tidy in a way that suits the look. A quick steam or lint roll often does more than swapping a piece.

7. Occasion and comfort

Think about the dress code, the weather and what you'll be doing. Can you sit, walk and carry things? Will you be too warm or too cold? An outfit that fails here will look worse by mid-afternoon.

Why your outfit feels off: symptoms and quick fixes

When every piece is nice but the whole thing feels wrong, match the feeling to the likely cause below.

What it looks likeLikely causeQuick fix
Flat or boringEverything is the same tone or textureAdd contrast, a textured layer or one accent color
Messy or busyToo many colors or patterns competingCut back to a base neutral plus one focal piece
Boxy or shapelessVolume on top and bottom, no defined waistTuck or half-tuck, add a belt, or swap one piece for a closer fit
Formality mismatchDressy top with casual shoes, or the reverseChange the shoes or outer layer to match
SloppyWrinkles, scuffs, uneven hemsSteam or press, clean shoes, fix or swap the hem
Looks like a costumeEvery piece follows the same theme exactlyBreak up the theme with one neutral or contrasting item

Change one thing at a time and re-check. If you swap three items at once, you won't know which change helped.

Check your outfit for the occasion

Work and interviews

Lean slightly more polished than the everyday office standard. Neat, well-fitted pieces in solid or subtle colors, clean shoes and minimal accessories are a safe base. Check that everything is pressed.

Dates and evenings out

Choose something that suits the venue. A relaxed bar suits dark jeans, a good top and clean boots, while a formal restaurant suggests tailored trousers or a dress and dressier shoes. Pick an outfit you won't need to adjust all night.

Casual days and events

For casual plans, it's usually better to dress up one notch than down. A clean tee with a light jacket and tidy trainers looks considered, while the same tee with stained joggers rarely does.

When in doubt, read the venue

Check the event invitation, the venue's website or photos of other guests, and ask the host if you're unsure. The dress code is often hinted at in the details.

Getting a second opinion on your outfit

Ask a trusted friend specific questions

"Is it okay?" gets you a polite yes. Better questions are "Do these shoes fit the rest?", "Is the top too long with these trousers?" or "Which of these two is better for tonight?"

Compare two options side by side

Take photos of both outfits in the same light and place them next to each other. Differences you can't feel in the mirror often jump out in a direct comparison.

Use an AI outfit checker as one more opinion

If you're alone or don't want to ask anyone, an AI outfit checker can give you quick feedback on things like color match and balance. Treat it as a starting point rather than a verdict; it isn't a professional stylist and can't know your taste, your event or your comfort.

Taste is subjective

Rules of color and proportion are guidelines, not laws. If you love a combination that breaks them and you feel great in it, that counts for a lot.

How FitCheck AI can help you check your outfit

  • Photo check: take or upload a clear, well-lit, head-to-toe photo that includes your shoes, and you get an instant fit check and an AI outfit score.

  • Live FitCheck: check an outfit live with the camera, with an outfit rating, color analysis, and matching and styling suggestions.

A 60-second final check before you head out

Screenshot this and run through it at the door:

  1. Shoes on, full-length mirror, good light.

hair-styles-for-curly-hair.body_html:
The best hair styles for curly hair work with your natural curl pattern instead of fighting it. That means a cut shaped around where your curls sit, a length chosen with shrinkage in mind, and a styling routine that keeps curls defined. Below are ideas for short, medium and long curls, easy everyday looks, occasion styles, men's cuts, and how to explain what you want to a hairdresser.

Start here: what makes a style work on curly hair

Curl pattern, density and shrinkage in plain terms

Curl pattern is the shape of your strands, from loose waves to tight coils. Density is how much hair you have on your head. Shrinkage is how much shorter your hair looks once it dries and the curls spring back. Hair that reaches your shoulders when wet can sit noticeably higher when dry, and tighter patterns usually shrink more.

This matters when you choose a length. A curly bob that looks chin-length when wet may land at the jaw or higher when dry. If you want a specific length, judge it by how your hair looks dry, not by how it hangs when stretched straight.

Why cut shape matters as much as styling

Curls tend to expand outward, so the overall silhouette is the main design choice. A rounded shape keeps volume even all over. A tapered shape keeps the sides slimmer and puts volume on top or at the ends. Layers remove weight, which can lift flat roots, but too many layers on fine or loosely curled hair can leave the ends wispy.

If you are unsure of your pattern

If you are not sure whether your hair is wavy, curly or coily, take the hair type quiz first. Knowing your pattern makes it easier to choose reference photos and describe your hair to a stylist.

Short curly hairstyles

Cropped curls and tapered sides

A cropped cut keeps the length on top, where curls can show, and tapers the sides and back. It is quick to manage, and it suits tighter patterns well because the curls are not weighed down by length.

Curly pixie

A curly pixie is longer on top with soft, short sides. It shows off your pattern and can work with many face shapes if the top length is balanced to your features. Leave enough length on top for curls to form rather than just stand up.

Curly bob

The curly bob is a popular choice. A chin-length bob looks neat and playful. A just-below-chin bob gives a little more weight, which can make shrinkage less dramatic. Stacked or rounded bobs add volume at the back, while a longer front adds a gentle angle.

What to ask for and what to watch with shrinkage

  • Ask your stylist to check where your curls sit when dry, then decide on length.
  • Go slightly longer than you imagine if you want to keep options open. Hair can be cut shorter later but not longer.
  • Request a shape (rounded, tapered or angled), not just a length.

Medium-length curly hairstyles

Layered lob

A lob (long bob) that grazes the collarbone, with soft layers, is a flexible shape. It can be worn down, tucked behind the ears, or pulled into a low bun. The layers stop the bottom from looking like a heavy triangle.

Curly shag and curly mullet

The curly shag uses lots of short layers on top with longer lengths below, which adds movement and volume. The curly mullet goes further, with a more distinct short top and a longer back. These are bolder choices that work best when shaped by a stylist who is comfortable cutting curls.

Curly fringe: full, side-swept or curtain-style

Yes, curly hair can have a fringe, but plan for shrinkage. A full fringe can look noticeably shorter when dry, so many people choose a fringe that starts a little longer. A side-swept fringe is more forgiving because it blends into the layers. A curtain-style fringe parts in the middle and frames the face, which can suit looser curls especially well.

Rounded shapes versus tapered shapes

If you like volume and have a longer face, a rounded shape adds width. If your hair feels wide at the sides, a tapered shape with more length on top can feel more balanced. There is no fixed rule, just proportion: decide which area you want to emphasise.

Long curly hairstyles

Long layers for volume and movement

Long layers keep length while stopping curls from collapsing into one heavy sheet. Shorter layers near the crown add lift, and longer ones blend into the ends for bounce.

One-length curls and where they can sit heavy

One-length cuts are simple and look graceful when the curl is loose and the hair is fine. On thicker or tighter curls, they can pile into a triangle shape, with volume at the bottom and flatness at the top. If that sounds familiar, ask for light layers.

Face-framing pieces

A few shorter strands around the face can soften a long style. Keep them long enough to avoid shrinking into awkward short tufts, and ask your stylist to judge the length on dry hair.

Easy everyday curly styles

StyleBest forEffort
Wash-and-goMost lengths and patternsLow once your routine is set
Twist-out or braid-outDefined, stretched curlsMedium, with prep the night before
Half-up with clipsGrowing out layers, mid to longVery low
Pineapple or high bunSecond-day hair, workoutsVery low
Headband or scarfRushed mornings, frizzy daysVery low

Wash-and-go

Apply your styling products to damp hair, shape the curls with your hands, then let them dry or use a diffuser on low heat. Try not to touch the hair while it dries to limit frizz.

Twist-out or braid-out

Twist or loosely braid damp, product-treated hair in sections, let it dry fully, then unravel gently. This gives stretched, defined curls with a different look from a wash-and-go.

Half-up styles and clips

A half-up style keeps hair off your face while showing off length. Claw clips and barrettes work well on thick curls.

Pineapple or high bun

Gather hair loosely at the top of your head with a soft tie. It keeps curls off your neck, and the shape is easy to shake out afterwards.

Headbands and scarves

A wide headband or a silk-style scarf adds polish to second-day curls and works as a styling accent.

Curly updos and styles for occasions

Work and interviews

A low bun with the front curls left out, or a neat half-up, looks professional while keeping your texture visible. A defined, tidy wash-and-go works too. Neatness at the hairline and ends matters more than straightening.

Weddings and parties

A loose, textured updo with a few curls left around the face looks elegant and relaxed. Add pins, a clip, or a ribbon for a finishing touch. Try your chosen style a week or two before the event so you know how it behaves.

Gym and rainy days

Braids, a pineapple bun, or a scarf-wrapped bun keep your shape together when you sweat or when the weather turns. A hooded jacket plus a loose style beats a tight tie.

Pairing a style with your outfit and neckline

  • Updos show off a V-neck, off-the-shoulder top or statement earrings.
  • Voluminous down curls balance structured or fitted pieces, like a tailored blazer.
  • High necklines (turtlenecks, collars) often look best with hair up or in a short cut so volume does not bunch around the neck.

Low-tension styles

Braids, twists and buns as styling options

Braids, twists and buns can be attractive ways to wear curls, especially when you want less daily styling. As a cosmetic choice, pick styles that feel comfortable rather than tight, and loosen anything that feels like it is pulling.

Keep it cosmetic

Curly hairstyles for men and short-hair routines

Tapers, fades and textured tops

A taper or fade with a longer, curly top is a classic. The shorter sides keep things tidy and highlight the curls above. Choose a low, mid or high fade depending on how sharp you want the contrast.

Curly fringe and longer top styles

A forward, textured fringe suits looser curls and creates a relaxed look. Longer curls on top can be swept to the side or worn up in a loose knot once they grow out.

Easy day-to-day styling

Apply a light styling product to damp hair, scrunch, and let it dry. Keep the sides trimmed regularly so the shape does not look overgrown.

Day-two refresh and keeping your style going

Re-shaping instead of re-washing

Mist hair lightly with water, scrunch in a little product, and re-form flattened curls with your fingers. Flip your head to restore volume at the roots, then let hair air-dry or diffuse briefly.

Sleeping on curls without ruining the shape

Tie hair in a loose pineapple, use a silk or satin pillowcase or bonnet, and avoid tight elastics. Many people find this helps curls keep their shape overnight.

When a trim helps the shape

If your style looks bottom-heavy, ends look uneven, or curls no longer sit where they used to, a trim can restore the shape. Timing varies from person to person, so decide based on how the shape looks rather than a fixed schedule.

How to choose and brief your hairdresser

Finding a stylist comfortable with curls

Look for a stylist who shows curly clients in their portfolio and asks about your routine. Many curl-focused stylists cut or check the shape on dry hair, so you can see how curls fall. Ask about their approach before you book.

Bringing photos of curl patterns similar to yours

A photo of a cut on hair that looks like yours is much more useful than one on straight hair. Bring two or three photos and note what you like in each, such as the fringe, the length or the volume.

Words to use

  • Layers: say whether you want light or visible ones.
  • Dry cut: ask if they can shape your hair dry or check it dry.
  • Weight: tell them if you want to keep or remove weight at the ends.
  • Fringe length: ask them to cut longer to allow for shrinkage.

If you are still deciding what suits you, our haircut decision guide walks through face shape, lifestyle and maintenance.

Preview a curly style before you commit

Photo setup

For hair previews, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level, and avoid filters.

Treat a preview as a rough guide

AI-generated previews are approximations. They may not capture exactly how your curls fall or shrink, so use them to narrow down ideas, not as a promise. A stylist's view of your actual hair should carry more weight. For more on this, read how to try hairstyles on your face before you commit to a cut.

How FitCheck AI can help

FitCheck AI offers hairstyle recommendations, which are AI suggestions for hairstyles to consider. Its AI hairstyle try-on generates AI images of you with a new hairstyle from your photo, so you can look at ideas such as a curly bob or a fringe before booking. The app also has hairstyle, curl and hair colour inspiration. It is cosmetic only and is not a stylist.

haircut-for-round-face-men.body_html:
The best haircut for a round face adds height on top and keeps the sides tight, so the face looks longer and more angular. A taper or skin fade with a textured quiff, crop or pompadour is the classic formula. Treat these as starting guidelines, not strict rules: plenty of men with round faces wear "wrong" cuts well.

How to know if you have a round face

A quick mirror check: length versus width

Pull your hair back and look straight at a mirror. A round face is usually close to equal in length and width, measured from hairline to chin and across the widest point of the cheekbones. The jaw tends to be soft rather than sharply angled, and the cheeks look full. If your face is clearly longer than it is wide, you are more likely oval or oblong.

Round vs. oval vs. square: the differences that matter for a cut

  • Round: similar length and width, soft jaw, full cheeks. Cuts that add vertical lines and definition help.
  • Oval: longer than wide, balanced proportions. Many cuts work, so you can choose by taste.
  • Square: similar length and width, but with a strong, angular jaw. The jaw already gives definition, so you have more freedom to go shorter or softer on the sides.

Why face shape is a loose guide, not a rule

Few faces fit one label perfectly. Hair type, density, hairline, glasses and personal style matter just as much. Use face shape to narrow your options, then let the details decide. For a broader method, see this 5-step guide to choosing a haircut.

What makes a haircut work on a round face

Add height on top

Volume above the forehead stretches the visual line of the face upward. About 3 to 4 inches of length on top that you can lift, sweep or push back usually does it, though the right amount depends on your hair type and density.

Keep the sides tighter

Hair that sits out at ear and cheek level adds width exactly where a round face already has it. Short sides, such as a taper or fade, remove that width and make the top stand out.

Use angles and texture

Soft, even, rounded outlines echo the shape of the face. Choppy texture, a diagonal fringe or a defined part adds contrast and breaks up the curves.

A sharp outline and clean neckline

Crisp edges around the temples, ears and neck give the head a more structured look. A neckline that grows out fuzzy can soften the shape you just built.

Short haircuts for round face men

Taper or skin fade with volume on top

This is one of the most popular options. A taper keeps a little length that gradually shortens toward the neckline, while a skin fade goes down to the skin. A mid or high fade removes the most side width, and a low fade is subtler. Pair either with about 3 to 4 inches on top, styled up and slightly back.

Textured crop with an angled fringe

A crop is short and choppy with a fringe. On a round face, ask for the fringe to sweep to one side rather than sit straight across, and for the texture to be cut in (point-cutting) so it does not look like a flat shelf.

Short quiff

Keep the front longer and lift it up and slightly back. Short sides keep the focus on height.

Crew cut and buzz cuts

A crew cut with a little length at the front, brushed up, works well. A very short, even buzz can emphasize the roundness of the head and face because it removes contrast. It can still look good, particularly with a beard or strong brow line, so consider it a trade-off, not a ban.

Medium-length hairstyles for round face men

Pompadour and slick-back with tight sides

Brushing hair up and back from the forehead creates strong vertical lines. Keep the sides faded or tapered so the volume stays on top.

Textured quiff or side-swept style

A bit more length than the short quiff gives you more movement. Style it up and to one side for an asymmetrical line.

Faux hawk or tousled upward styles

Pushing the center of the top upward lengthens the face. Keep the sides short so it reads as intentional, not messy.

Longer top with an undercut

An undercut has very short sides with a clear disconnection to longer hair on top. Worn slicked back or swept up, it gives the most contrast of any cut here. Ask your barber how disconnected you want it.

Longer hair and a round face: what to watch

Layers and length past the chin versus side volume

Long hair can work if it falls fairly straight past the chin, because that creates vertical lines. Trouble starts when volume gathers between cheekbone and jaw height, such as bushy waves or short layers that flare out beside the face. Ask your barber to remove bulk from the sides and keep the length hanging down rather than out.

Pulling hair up or back

Slicking hair back or tying it up creates vertical lines, but it also shows the sides of your head. It works best when the sides are tapered or kept neat. If the sides are full and fluffy, pulling hair back can emphasize width instead.

Man bun or top knot

Place the knot high on the crown rather than low at the nape. A high knot adds height. Tapered sides will sharpen the look further.

Fringes, parts and hairlines

Side part versus center part

A side part creates a diagonal line that breaks up the roundness. A deep side part with volume swept up is a safe choice. A center part can work with longer, straight hair, but it frames the face symmetrically and may emphasize its width.

Textured, angled fringe versus heavy blunt fringe

A fringe that is choppy and swept sideways adds angles. A thick, straight-across fringe cuts the face into a shorter shape and can make it look rounder.

Styling around a receding or higher hairline

This is purely about style. Brushing hair up and back, or choosing a short textured crop, can suit a higher hairline. If you have any concern about your hair or scalp, see a doctor or dermatologist. A haircut guide cannot answer that.

Haircuts to approach with caution

Bowl-style and even, rounded cuts

Hair the same length all over, cut in a soft round outline, mirrors the face shape.

Heavy blunt fringes

As above, these shorten the face visually.

Wide, flat volume at the sides

Hair that grows out sideways over the ears adds width. This is common when a cut grows out.

Why "avoid" lists are only guides

A good barber can adjust any of these: shorter sides, a longer top, a diagonal fringe. If you love a style on the list, ask how it could be tweaked for your face.

Beards and glasses with a round face

Shorter on the cheeks, a bit longer at the chin

Keeping the cheeks short and leaving more length at the chin makes the face look longer and adds a sense of jawline. A full, even beard that is wide at the sides can add width.

Clean cheek lines, neckline and hairline balance

Define the cheek line with a clean edge and trim the neckline above the Adam's apple. Let your sideburns blend into the fade or taper so the hair and beard read as one shape. Fuzzy lines blur the structure you are trying to create.

Frames

Angular or rectangular frames add contrast to soft curves. Very round frames can echo the shape of the face, although many people like that look, so let comfort and taste guide you.

Match the cut to your hair type and climate

If you are not sure of your hair type, this short hair type quiz can help you describe it to your barber.

  • Thick and straight: ask for bulk to be thinned at the sides and keep the top controlled so it does not spread outward.
  • Fine: use a matte texture product and lift at the roots, because fine hair can lose height easily.
  • Wavy and curly: let the top curl naturally for volume and keep the sides tight with a taper or fade.
  • Hot and humid weather: ask for short tapered sides, which keep the neck cooler, and a textured top that holds its shape without much product. Use a small amount of lightweight matte product. Humidity can still make wavy or curly hair frizz and fine hair go flat, so lift the front again with your fingers during the day.

How to style your cut for height

  1. Blow-dry upward and back from the roots. Use your fingers or a brush to lift the front while the hair is damp.
  2. Choose a matte clay, paste or powder. Start with a pea-sized amount, warm it between your palms, and add more only if needed. Too much can weigh hair down.
  3. Finish in about two minutes. Dry, apply product, shape the front up and to the side, and check that the sides sit flat.

Preview your shortlist before you cut

Pick two or three styles from this guide. Then take a clear, front-facing photo: face natural light, hold the camera at eye level, and skip filters. What to tell your barber

Bring reference photos

Choose photos of people with similar hair type and density to yours. A style that looks great on thick, straight hair may not work on fine, wavy hair.

Words to use

Disconnected / undercutShort sides with a clear step up to longer hair on top.
NecklineThe shape at the back: blocked, rounded or tapered.

Ask about upkeep

Ask how to style it at home and how often to trim. Fades usually look their best with frequent touch-ups, and your barber can tell you what is realistic for your hair.

A copy-and-paste barber brief

"I have a round face and [thick/fine/wavy/curly] hair. I'd like a [low/mid] taper or skin fade on the sides, about 3 to 4 inches on top, textured with point-cutting, and styled up and to one side. Please keep the fringe angled, not blunt, and clean up the neckline. How should I style it, and how often should I come back?"

how-to-organize-your-closet.body_html:
To organize your closet, take everything out, sort it into keep, maybe, donate, repair and out-of-season piles, group what stays by category, then store it so your most-worn pieces are the easiest to reach. Most of the work is deciding what earns a place, not buying containers. The steps below work for a walk-in, a small reach-in, or a closet you share.

Before you start: set a goal and block out the time

Decide what "organized" means for you. It might be faster mornings, more free space, or wearing more of what you already own. Your goal shapes your choices later. If you want faster mornings, for example, you will be stricter about pieces you never reach for.

Quick tidy or full reset?

A quick tidy (refolding, rehanging, removing obvious donations) can take under an hour. A full reset, where every item comes out, is better for a closet that feels overwhelming, and it usually needs a free half day. If you can't spare that, work one section at a time, such as shelves on Saturday and hanging clothes on Sunday.

What you need

  • Bags or boxes labeled donate, repair and out-of-season
  • A full-length mirror and good light
  • A clear floor or bed to lay things out on
  • Matching hangers, if you have them

Step 1: Take everything out (or one section at a time)

Seeing everything at once shows you duplicates, forgotten pieces and how much you actually own. If the closet is big, empty one zone at a time: all hanging tops, then bottoms, then shelves, then shoes. Once a section is empty, wipe down the shelves and rod and vacuum the floor before anything goes back in. A clean, empty space also helps you picture a better layout.

Step 2: Sort into keep, maybe, donate, repair and out-of-season

Pick up each piece and ask a few plain questions:

  • Does it fit now? Not "it might fit someday", but how it fits today.
  • Is it comfortable? If you keep adjusting it, you probably won't wear it.
  • Is it in good condition? Look for pilling, stretched necklines, stains, loose hems and missing buttons.
  • Do I have somewhere to wear it? A great jacket doesn't help if your life has no place for it.
  • Would I choose it again today? This question settles most borderline cases.

The try-on test for borderline pieces

If you can't decide, try the piece on in front of a mirror in good light, with the shoes you'd normally wear. Check whether it sits well on the shoulders, whether the length is where you want it, and whether the color looks good near your face. If you need a better understanding of which shades suit you, our guide to finding your skin tone depth and undertone can help.

Handle the "maybe" pile with a date

Put maybes in a box and write a review date on it, about three months out. If you haven't taken anything out of the box by then, donate it. This keeps you from getting stuck while sparing you the pressure of deciding on the spot.

Sentimental and "someday" clothes

You don't have to get rid of these, but they shouldn't take up prime hanging space. Give them one box or one shelf, kept apart from the clothes you wear every week.

Get donations and repairs out of the house

Put the donation bag in your car or by the door the same day. For repairs, set a deadline, for instance two weeks. Anything not mended by then goes to donation.

Step 3: Group what you're keeping

Start with category: tops, bottoms, dresses, outerwear, and so on. Within each category, sort by whatever fits how you dress:

  • Color: works well if you pick outfits by color. Go light to dark within each group.
  • Sleeve length or garment length: short sleeves before long sleeves, or shorter skirts before longer ones. This makes layering choices easier.
  • Occasion: if your life splits cleanly into work, casual, workout and event clothes, give each its own zone.

Category first, then color is the simplest default. Add the occasion split only if you really do dress in separate modes.

Step 4: Choose storage that suits your clothes and your space

Hang or fold?

Usually hang:

  • Blazers and coats
  • Dress shirts
  • Dresses
  • Trousers, especially if you want to keep a crease

Usually fold:

  • Knitwear and sweaters (hanging can stretch the shoulders)
  • T-shirts
  • Jeans
  • Workout clothes

Treat this as general guidance. Check care labels, and adjust for how much rod and shelf space you have.

Don't overcrowd

If you have to push hangers apart to see a garment, the rod is too full. Matching hangers keep the line tidy and make it easier to scan what you own. Leave a hand's width of room so clothes don't wrinkle against each other.

Shelves, drawers and bins

Fold knits and tees into stacks you can see from the side, so you don't need to dig. Use bins for like items (belts, scarves, gym gear), and use the vertical space above the rod for out-of-season or occasion items. Keep like with like, so there's always one obvious place for each thing.

Shoes, bags, belts, scarves and jewelry

  • Put everyday shoes at floor level or on a low rack, and rarely worn pairs higher up.
  • Hang belts and scarves on hooks or a slim hanger so you can see them all.
  • Stand bags upright (stuffed lightly so they hold their shape) rather than piling them.
  • Use a shallow tray or divided drawer for jewelry so pieces don't tangle.

Small or shared closets

In a small closet, use double-hang rods for shorter items like shirts and skirts, and move off-season clothes under the bed or on a top shelf. In a shared closet, divide it by side or by shelf, and keep a small overflow zone so neither person's clothes spill into the other's space.

Step 5: Place things by how often you wear them

Keep everyday pieces between shoulder and knee height, where you can reach them without bending or stretching. Move the rarely worn pieces higher or lower. This one rule makes a closet feel much easier to use.

Seasonal rotation

To organize clothes by season, store the pieces you won't need for a few months in labeled bins or garment bags. Clean everything before storing it. Swap at the change of season, and use the swap as your chance to reassess what you didn't wear last time. Leave transitional layers, like a light jacket or a cardigan, in the main closet all year.

Formalwear and occasion pieces

Suits, gowns and formal shoes should live together at one end of the rod, in breathable garment bags if possible, so they stay in good shape and are easy to find when needed.

Step 6: Turn a tidy closet into outfits you'll wear

An organized closet only pays off if it helps you get dressed. Spend ten minutes building three to five outfits from what you kept, and notice which pieces appear again and again.

Use simple outfit formulas

  • Smart casual: navy blazer + white tee + straight-leg jeans + white sneakers.
  • Relaxed layers: olive overshirt + cream tee + dark trousers + brown boots.
  • Balanced proportions: wide-leg trousers + fitted top, or an oversized sweater + slim trousers. Pairing loose with fitted usually works better than loose with loose, though an all-oversized look can be a deliberate choice.

Pairings that tend to work: camel with navy, charcoal with burgundy, cream with olive, and black with white or gray. Keeping a few neutrals as your base makes everything easier to mix.

Spot gaps before buying anything

If you keep building outfits that need a neutral layer, a versatile shoe, or a missing color, write it down. That list is far more useful than shopping without a plan, and it stops you from adding more things you won't wear.

A simple capsule approach

A capsule wardrobe closet is just a core of mix-and-match pieces in colors that work together. Choose two or three neutrals plus one or two accent colors, then check that most tops work with most bottoms. When you're unsure how to start your day, our 5-step guide to deciding what to wear today pairs well with a freshly organized closet.

How to keep your closet organized

  • One in, one out: when something new comes in, something leaves.
  • A 10-minute monthly reset: rehang, refold, and move anything out of place.
  • A twice-a-year review: do it at the seasonal swap and look for items you never wore.
  • Check the maybe box: on its review date, decide on everything inside it.

Where FitCheck AI can help (Android)

A physical closet still needs your hands, and no app will sort it for you. But once it's tidy, FitCheck AI can support the next step. Its digital closet and wardrobe organizer lets you organize clothes by season or occasion, save favorite and top-scoring looks, build a capsule wardrobe and plan outfits ahead for work, weekends or events.

If you're unsure about a borderline piece, you can also upload a clear, well-lit, head-to-toe photo that includes your shoes and get an AI outfit score with a breakdown of color match, proportion and balance. Treat that as a second opinion, not a professional stylist's verdict or an objective answer. The app is free on Google Play for Android, and iOS is coming soon.

how-to-test-hair-porosity.body_html:
To test hair porosity at home, start with clean, product-free hair and try two or three simple checks: the float test, the slip-and-slide strand test and the spray bottle test. Compare the results to see whether your hair tends toward low, medium or high porosity. These tests are rough guides, not lab measurements, so treat the outcome as a starting point for choosing products and styling habits.

What hair porosity is (and what it isn't)

Porosity describes how readily your hair takes in and holds onto moisture. Each strand is covered in overlapping scales called the cuticle. When the cuticle lies flat and tight, water and products tend to enter slowly. When it is raised or uneven, they tend to enter quickly and may leave just as fast.

Porosity vs. hair type, strand width and density

Porosity is not the same as hair type. Your type (straight, wavy, curly or coily) describes the shape of the strand and the curl pattern. Strand width is how thick each hair is, and density is how many hairs you have. Two people with identical curl patterns can have very different porosity. If you are not sure of your type yet, take the hair type quiz first, then come back here.

Why people want to know it

The practical reason is product choice and routine: how heavy a cream to use, how to apply it, and how much heat feels right. It is a styling characteristic, not a measure of whether your hair or scalp is healthy.

Prep first: how to get a fair result

Many unreliable results come from skipping preparation. Product residue can change how water behaves on a strand, and oils can affect whether it floats, which can skew almost every test.

Start with clean hair free of oils, conditioner and styling products

Wash with a clarifying or regular shampoo, rinse well, and let your hair dry completely without applying conditioner, oil, leave-in or gel. Wait until the next day if you can, so you are testing your hair and not your products.

Collect strands from different areas

Use a few strands rather than just one, and pull them from different areas if possible. Hair near your crown, your nape and the ends of your lengths can behave differently, especially if parts of your hair are colored or heat-styled. Strands that have shed naturally, for example from your brush, are the easiest to collect, but they may not behave exactly like hair that is still on your head, and hair snipped from your head may give a slightly different result again. Treat any sample as a rough guide.

Test more than once and use more than one method

One test is a snapshot. Running two or three methods, and repeating one of them on another day, gives you a fuller picture than any single result.

Test 1: The float test (treat it with caution)

Step-by-step method

  1. Fill a clear glass with room-temperature water.
  2. Drop in a few clean, dry strands (three or four is better than one), ideally from different areas of your head.
  3. Watch for a few minutes without stirring or touching the glass.
  4. Note whether most of the strands float, hover in the middle or sink to the bottom. If they behave differently from each other, note that too.

How people usually read the result

Strands that stay at the top are often read as lower porosity. Strands that sink quickly are often read as higher porosity. Strands that hover in the middle are often read as medium.

Why it can mislead

The float test is popular but far from definitive. Leftover product, natural oils, the weight of a single strand, the surface tension of the water and how long you wait can all change the outcome. Shed hair may also differ from hair cut from your head. A strand that looks like it floats may simply be coated in residue. Use this test as one clue among several.

Test 2: The slip-and-slide strand test

Step-by-step method

  1. Take a clean, dry strand and pinch it between the thumb and forefinger of one hand, near the tip end, to hold it steady.
  2. With the thumb and forefinger of your other hand, pinch the strand a little further along and slide your fingers up the strand toward the root end (the end that was closest to your scalp).
  3. Notice whether your fingers glide smoothly or catch on bumps and roughness.

What the feel generally suggests

A smooth glide is often associated with a tighter, flatter cuticle, which tends to go with lower porosity. A bumpy or rough feel is often associated with a more raised cuticle, which tends to go with higher porosity.

Limits

Roughness can also come from product buildup, heat styling, chemical processing or simply the natural texture of your hair. Because the result is based on feel, it is subjective, so compare it with another test before drawing conclusions.

Test 3: The spray bottle or water absorption test

Step-by-step method

  1. Start with clean, fully dry hair and no products.
  2. Section off a small piece of hair and lightly spritz it with plain water.
  3. Watch what the water does over the next minute or two.

What the result tends to suggest

If water beads up on the surface and sits there before soaking in, your hair may lean toward lower porosity. If the hair soaks up water almost instantly and feels wet through quickly, it may lean toward higher porosity. Gradual, even absorption sits in the middle.

Why it works best on freshly clean hair

Any coating on the hair can make water bead up, so this test is only meaningful on freshly cleansed strands. Try it on a few different sections of your head, since the ends often absorb differently from the roots.

Reading your results: low, medium or high porosity

What you might notice

ObservationOften points to low porosityOften points to medium porosityOften points to high porosity
Float testStrands stay on topStrands hover in the middleStrands sink fast
Slip-and-slideFeels smoothMostly smooth, slight textureFeels bumpy or rough
Spray bottleWater beads on the hairAbsorbs steadilySoaks in right away
Everyday behaviorSlow to get wet, slow to dry, products can sit on topModerate drying time, usually holds stylesWets and dries fast, tends toward frizz, products seem to vanish

What to do if your tests disagree

This is common. Give more weight to how your hair behaves day to day: how long it takes to dry, whether products sit on top or disappear, and how it handles humidity. If the tests still conflict, you may have a mix, such as a smoother root area and rougher, more processed ends.

Porosity differs across your head and changes over time

Coloring, bleaching, heat styling, sun, weather and even rough brushing can all shift how your hair behaves. Older, more processed lengths often differ from newer growth near the scalp. Retest every few months, or after a big change like a new color, and treat each result as a snapshot.

What to do with your result: general styling guidance

This is cosmetic routine guidance only. Adjust it to what you see in your own hair, since results vary from person to person.

Low porosity

  • Choose lightweight products such as lotions, mousses and light gels over thick butters and heavy oils.
  • Apply products to damp hair. Some people find gentle warmth, such as a warm towel, helps products spread.
  • Avoid layering many products, which can leave hair feeling coated or weighed down.

Medium porosity

  • This type is usually flexible, so a simple routine of a cleanser, a conditioner and a styler often works.
  • Keep an eye on changes after coloring or frequent heat.

High porosity

  • Try richer creams and butters. Some people also like to follow a water-based product with a light oil or butter to help it last, but how well this works varies, so see whether it suits your hair before making it a habit.
  • Use lower heat settings and a heat protectant, and keep brushing gentle.
  • If your hair dries quickly, you can optionally apply products while it is still very wet, then see whether the finish suits you.

What these tests can't tell you

They say nothing about hair or scalp health

Porosity tests only describe how your strands take in water. Nothing in this article is medical advice, and FitCheck AI's feedback is cosmetic and not medical advice either, so please see a dermatologist or doctor for any concern about your hair or scalp.

When to get professional advice

Talk to a doctor or dermatologist if you notice a sudden change in texture, unusual shedding, scalp pain, irritation or patches. A porosity test cannot explain those changes.

From porosity to a look you love

Once you know how your hair behaves, use that to choose a style that suits it. Pair your porosity result with your curl pattern from the hair type quiz, then read our guide to choosing a haircut that suits you and your texture and face shape. Low porosity hair that dries slowly may suit a style that needs less daily product. Higher porosity hair that frizzes in humidity may suit a cut that works with air-drying. When you have a shortlist, you can preview hairstyles on your face before committing.

How FitCheck AI can help with your hair look

To be clear, FitCheck AI is not a porosity test and does not measure porosity. What it can help with is the next step: turning what you know about your hair into a look. You can explore hairstyle, curl and hair color inspiration, get AI hairstyle recommendations, and use live hair analysis with the camera for cosmetic hairstyle and hair color ideas. You can also try different hairstyles on your own face, as the app generates AI images of you with a new hairstyle from your photo. Treat these as a visual starting point and a second opinion, not a professional stylist's advice.

makeup-virtual-try-on-guide.body_html:
A makeup virtual try-on uses your phone camera to layer digital color, such as a lipstick shade, onto a live image of your face so you can preview a look before you apply anything. It works best as a quick way to compare colors and overall effect, not as a promise of how a specific product will look or wear. This guide covers how to get a realistic preview and how to turn it into a real-life decision.

What a makeup virtual try-on is (and what it isn't)

How a live camera preview works in plain terms

In general, these tools use your camera to find your face, then place a color over areas of the face. Which areas are supported depends on the tool. Because the preview is live, you can turn your head, smile and change expression to see how the color moves with you. Think of it as a mirror that lets you test ideas without a makeup bag.

What it's good for: color, placement and overall effect

A preview is useful for quick answers to questions like these:

  • Does a warm coral lip look balanced with my coloring, or does a cooler rose suit me better?
  • Does a bold lip feel too heavy, or does it feel like a polished finish?
  • Does the overall effect feel soft and everyday, or more dramatic?
  • Which of these two looks feels right for a work day versus an evening out?

What it can't show: texture, finish, wear and formula behavior

A screen can't reproduce how a product feels or behaves on skin. Use the table below to set your expectations.

A preview can help withA preview can't tell you
General color family and intensityExact shade or how a specific product will look
Placement and overall effectTexture, coverage and how a formula sits on your skin
Whether a look suits the occasionHow long it lasts or how it fades through the day
Comparing two or three ideas quicklyHow a color reads in every kind of light

Set up for a realistic preview

Face natural light and hold the camera at eye level

Stand facing a window so daylight falls evenly on your face. Hold the phone at eye level. A camera held low adds shadows under the chin and nose, and those shadows muddy lip colors.

Skip beauty filters and heavy retouching

Smoothing and brightening filters change your skin tone on screen, so any color you try on top will look different from real life. Turn them off to get the most honest view.

Start from a clean or neutral base so colors read clearly

If you're wearing heavy lipstick or bold eye makeup, the preview will blend with it. A bare or lightly done face gives the cleanest read of how a new color looks.

Check on more than one screen brightness

Screen brightness changes how saturated a color appears. Look at your favorite option at a medium and a high brightness. If it looks good at both, that is a good sign.

Before you try colors: know your starting point

Undertone and depth in one minute

Depth is how light or deep your skin is. Undertone is the cool, warm or neutral tint beneath the surface. As a loose starting point, cooler undertones often look balanced in berry, rose and blue-leaning pinks, while warmer undertones often suit coral, peach and terracotta. If you're unsure where you land, our guide on how to find your skin depth and undertone walks through it.

How contrast level changes what looks balanced

Contrast is the difference between your hair, skin and eye color. High contrast, such as dark hair with fair skin, can usually carry a defined lip like deep red or plum. Softer contrast, such as light brown hair with medium skin, often looks harmonious with softer tones like a muted rose or a brown-leaning nude.

Why this is a loose guide, not a rule

Plenty of people look great in colors that break these guidelines. Use undertone and contrast to choose what to try first, then let the preview and your own taste decide.

How to try makeup virtually, step by step

  1. Start with one change. A lip color is the easiest place to begin because it makes the biggest difference with the least guesswork.
  2. Compare a few shades side by side. Try something like a warm nude, a rosy pink and a deeper berry. Changing only one variable at a time makes it easier to see what you actually prefer.
  3. Look up close and at arm's length. Up close shows intensity. At arm's length you see how the look reads to other people.
  4. Think about the rest of the look. Once a lip works, picture what you'd wear with it, such as a cheek color in the same warm or cool family. Keep it simple, and note that which products you can preview depends on the tool you use.
  5. Keep a short list of your top two or three. Take a screenshot with your phone's own screenshot function, or jot down a description of each, such as "warm rosy-brown, medium intensity." A short list is much easier to act on than a pile of maybes.

How to judge a preview honestly

Does it suit your coloring, or just the lighting?

If a color only looks good under one lamp or at one angle, treat it with caution. Recheck near a window and see whether it still looks flattering.

Does the look match the occasion and your outfit?

A bold red lip can feel great with a simple black top and feel overwhelming with a busy print. Once you've settled on a look, you can also check how it sits with what you're wearing. The virtual outfit try-on feature shows AI-generated images of you in different outfits from your photo, which can help you picture the whole look together.

Does it feel like you, and is it easy to recreate?

A look you can't replicate on a regular morning isn't very useful. If a preview needs three products and a steady hand for winged liner, ask whether you'll really do that. A simple lip and cheek combination often wins for everyday wear. If you're still deciding which looks to try, our self-guided quiz on what makeup suits your face is a good place to start.

From screen to real life

Swatch-test before committing

Test the real product on your jawline or inner wrist in daylight. The jawline is closer to your face color, while the wrist is easier to compare several shades on at once.

Match finish and intensity to the preview

Decide what you liked in the preview: a sheer wash of color, a satin finish or a full-coverage matte. Then look for a formula that matches that effect. A sheer tint and an opaque matte can be the same color on screen and very different on your lips.

Use your favorite preview as a reference, not a shade promise

Show your screenshot to a friend or a beauty counter artist as a mood reference. Describe it in words too, for example: a warm rosy-brown, medium intensity, soft finish. That gives them something to work with, and you still get to see the real product on your skin.

Common reasons a preview looks different in person

Screen color and brightness settings

Phones display color differently, and night modes or warm-tone settings shift everything. A coral can look orange on one phone and pink on another.

Indoor lighting versus daylight

Warm indoor bulbs add yellow, which makes cool pinks look duller. Cool white lights can make warm shades look flat. This is why a daylight check matters.

Sheer versus opaque formulas

A preview usually shows one level of color, while real products range from sheer to fully opaque. Your natural lip color also shows through sheer formulas and changes the end result.

How FitCheck AI can help you try makeup virtually

FitCheck AI is an Android app with several features that fit this process:

  • Live virtual makeup try-on: preview makeup looks, such as lipstick, on your own face with the live camera.
  • Makeup assist with live camera guidance while you work on a look.
  • AI makeup assistant: personalized suggestions and feedback on makeup looks, from an everyday glow to full glam, based on your appearance.
  • Live skin analysis (optional): an AI overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. This is not medical advice.

Lipstick is the example of a live try-on look that the app confirms. This guide doesn't assume that other products, such as blush or eye makeup, or saving looks inside the app, are available. For the best result, follow the same photo advice as above: face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and avoid filters. The app is free on Google Play for Android, and iOS is coming soon.

Good to know

Previews and AI feedback are a second opinion and a starting point. They are not a substitute for a professional makeup artist, and the scores and suggestions are AI opinion rather than fact. Skin feedback here is cosmetic only. If you have any concern about your skin, such as irritation, breakouts or a changing mole, please see a dermatologist or doctor.

If you also want to experiment with your hair, the same approach works there: try hairstyles on your face before you commit to a cut.
